title: Field treatment that safely stops inaccessible internal bleeding

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that an emergency responder could administer to stop bleeding inside the body when the injured vessel or organ cannot be exposed or directly compressed. It would provide selective, durable hemostasis across a useful range of injuries, including severe arterial and organ bleeding, while preserving the patient's ability to undergo later surgical repair. Treatment without locating or exposing the individual wound is an intended capability. A dressing that requires placement directly onto an exposed wound falls outside this scope.

Conceptual synthesis. Delivery into a body cavity and delivery through the bloodstream represent distinct approaches. A cavity-administered material would need to reach and control bleeding within the treated space. A bloodstream-delivered agent would need to act selectively at injured sites while circulating elsewhere. Evidence for one approach would establish only the capabilities actually demonstrated with that route, injury model, and treatment conditions.

significance.text: Conditional significance. If responders could safely control otherwise inaccessible hemorrhage before surgical access, some patients could survive injuries that currently require urgent operative bleeding control. The direct benefit would be earlier control during the interval between injury and definitive care, particularly where transport or access to surgery is delayed. How much hemorrhage care could move to the point of injury would depend on the range of treatable injuries, the time required for treatment to work, and clinical outcomes.

Conditional downstream possibilities. Durable bleeding control could give clinicians more time to transport, resuscitate, and prepare a patient for repair. Its impact would depend on whether control persists during movement and delayed surgery, and whether treatment preserves tissue and surgical access. Definitive repair could still be necessary. The supplied material does not establish a survival effect, the proportion of trauma patients who might benefit, or a general replacement for operative hemorrhage control.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability combines reliable control of inaccessible bleeding with selectivity, durability, tissue safety, and compatibility with subsequent repair. Demonstrating these properties together across a useful range of severe arterial and organ injuries is the central challenge. The supplied record does not establish whether this full capability remained unavailable as of November 1, 2026, because it contains no current evidence survey.

Engineering synthesis. Treatment must act effectively despite limited access to the wound and uncertainty about its location. Concrete barriers include reaching the bleeding region, stopping substantial blood loss, maintaining control until definitive care, and avoiding dangerous clotting elsewhere. Performance across different injury sites and severities cannot be inferred from success in a single model. The intended range of injuries therefore needs explicit definition.

Engineering synthesis. Delivery route changes the safety and performance problem. An intracavity treatment must control bleeding without unacceptable effects on nearby organs or interference with surgical access. A bloodstream-delivered treatment must achieve sufficient activity at an injury while preserving safe circulation elsewhere. Both approaches require evidence that hemorrhage control persists and that treatment leaves later repair feasible. These are proposed engineering requirements derived from the concept.

current_state.text: The reconciled research identifies an April 2024 Surgery article by Dorken-Gallastegi and colleagues, titled Safety of the injectable expanding biopolymer foam for non-compressible truncal bleeding in swine, with DOI 10.1016/j.surg.2023.11.010. According to that research account, the safety study placed an expanding chitosan polymer into the abdomen of pigs with mild closed-cavity splenic bleeding. Seven of eight treated animals reportedly survived to 28 days. One animal was reportedly terminated early and had superficial colonic ulcers. These details are retained as a reported experimental account whose underlying text was unavailable to the supplied review.

Access and verification are limited. The research states that an initial pass inspected the abstract's Methods and Results, followed by a recheck that encountered a journal access response of 403. The source index contains bibliographic information and the abstract URL, with no retained source text or artifacts. Consequently, the supplied review could not independently confirm the polymer composition, injury severity, animal counts, follow-up duration, or colonic findings. This missing-material limitation leaves those details unverified and provides no evidence contradicting the reported result.

Even if the reported details are confirmed, a small safety study involving mild splenic bleeding would establish a narrow experimental scope. The seven-of-eight survival count alone cannot establish a treatment-related survival benefit without the study's comparator and design information. The reported ulcer finding would require its study context to assess severity and attribution. This account does not establish efficacy across diverse lethal injuries, severe arterial hemorrhage, prolonged field use, or delivery through the bloodstream to a bleeding site.

The supplied evidence ends with this dated study account and its access limitations. It contains no documented human or prehospital results, independent replication, or later evidence establishing the full proposed capability. Its limited coverage also leaves the broader state of the field as of November 1, 2026 unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Blinded, independently replicated large-animal studies should test hemorrhage control and survival across multiple realistic injury sites and severities, including severe arterial and organ bleeding. Studies should incorporate delayed surgery and assess whether bleeding control lasts through the intended delay. Each delivery route should receive its own demonstration, with the treatment procedure and injury conditions documented sufficiently for independent reproduction.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated large-animal studies demonstrate durable hemorrhage control across injuries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements. Evaluation should include time to hemorrhage control, continued or recurrent bleeding, survival, thrombosis away from the injury, tissue damage, and feasibility of subsequent surgical repair. A complete protocol would need operational definitions of successful control, acceptable adverse effects, and the required duration of benefit. Acceptance thresholds should be specified before testing. The supplied material proposes this evaluation framework without establishing numerical thresholds or recognized standards.
completion_criteria.label: Report efficacy and safety outcomes against prespecified acceptance thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration. Multicenter prehospital trials should then test whether treatment improves survival and functional outcomes under realistic conditions, including long transport times. The resulting evidence should define practical boundaries such as supported injury locations, treatment timing, delivery route, and duration before definitive care. Finite studies can establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. Claims extending beyond the tested range would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Multicenter prehospital trials demonstrate improved survival and functional outcomes

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. EMR-01, Reversible emergency metabolic suspension, shares the aim of extending the opportunity for definitive treatment. EMR-03 targets continued blood loss, while EMR-01 concerns temporary metabolic suppression. EMR-02, Neurologically intact recovery after prolonged untreated cardiac arrest, concerns recovery after a prolonged interruption of circulation. Effective hemorrhage control could contribute to some resuscitation pathways, but would not by itself establish metabolic suspension or neurologically intact recovery after prolonged arrest.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-04, Inexpensive, universally compatible emergency blood replacement, addresses replacement of lost blood's functions. EMR-03 addresses control of the source of loss. The capabilities could complement each other during resuscitation. EMR-05, A portable, broad-spectrum emergency diagnostic system, could help identify internal bleeding and guide treatment. The aspiration to treat without locating the individual wound still leaves a role for diagnosis in determining eligibility and assessing response.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-06, Rapid reversal of septic shock and its harmful host response, and EMR-07, Broad-spectrum emergency antidote platform, also seek rapid treatment during time-critical emergencies. Their targets are the harmful host response in sepsis and toxic exposures, respectively. Shared delivery or emergency-use constraints would not establish a shared therapeutic mechanism or transferable efficacy.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-08, Non-surgical rescue oxygenation for otherwise unmanageable airways, addresses oxygen delivery when airway management fails. It could complement hemorrhage treatment in a patient with multiple injuries. EMR-09, Effective early prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder after emergency care, and EMR-10, Rapid, potent non-opioid treatment for severe acute pain, concern psychological and pain outcomes that require their own interventions and evidence.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-11, Acute rescue and repair of injured vital tissue, overlaps with the need to preserve organs during hemorrhage and subsequent care. EMR-03 focuses on arresting blood loss while preserving later repair. Demonstrating hemostasis would leave tissue rescue, regeneration, and restoration of organ function as separate capabilities to evaluate.

Comparator details, study design, and adverse-event context remain unavailable, limiting interpretation of survival and the attribution of tissue injury.
The supplied record does not establish the field's state or availability of the complete capability as of November 1, 2026.

brief.title: Emergency treatment to stop hidden internal bleeding
possible: After a serious injury, an emergency responder could stop bleeding inside the body without exposing or pressing on the wound, even without locating it precisely. The treatment would keep bleeding under control until surgery and leave damaged organs and vessels repairable.
why: People bleeding internally could gain time to reach surgery, especially when transport is slow. Earlier bleeding control could help some patients survive injuries that require urgent surgery today.
Clinicians would have more time to restore circulation and prepare for repair.

sources.showed: This was a safety study of expanding foam injected into the abdomen of pigs with mild spleen bleeding.
sources.cited_for: It supports studying the safety of foam delivered into the abdomen.
sources.not_established: A small study of mild bleeding cannot establish reliable control of severe injuries or a survival benefit.

sources.who: Leon Naar and colleagues at Massachusetts General Hospital and Medcura
sources.showed: Expanding foam injected into the abdomen improved short-term survival in pigs with otherwise lethal bleeding around the liver.
sources.quote:
Intraperitoneal administration of hm-chitosan-based foam for massive, noncompressible
abdominal bleeding improves survival in a lethal, closed-cavity swine model.
sources.cited_for: Foam delivered into the abdomen can improve survival in a severe animal injury model.
sources.not_established: The experiment does not establish lasting safety, effectiveness across different injuries, or benefit in people.

sources.showed: Injected particles that mimic platelets, the blood components that help form clots, reduced blood loss and improved short-term survival after an artery injury in pigs.
sources.quote:
Subsequently we demonstrated that, following femoral artery injury, bolus administration of
SynthoPlate could reduce blood loss, stabilize blood pressure and significantly improve survival.
sources.cited_for: Treatment through the bloodstream can reduce traumatic arterial bleeding in an animal model.
sources.not_established: This pilot study does not establish lasting control of hidden internal injuries or safety across a broad range of injuries.

sources.showed: A different injected particle formulation failed to reduce blood loss in pigs. Some animals developed clots in uninjured organs, and survival fell.
sources.quote: There are no significant differences in blood loss over the time period studied for any of the groups.
sources.cited_for: Treatments intended to promote clotting can cause dangerous clots away from an injury.
sources.not_established: These findings concern this formulation; they do not establish that every treatment delivered through the bloodstream has the same risks.

shown: Massachusetts General Hospital and Medcura researchers improved short-term survival using expanding foam inside pigs' abdomens after severe bleeding around the liver. This demonstrates benefit in a lethal animal injury model.

Hickman and colleagues reduced arterial bleeding with particles injected into the bloodstream in a small pig study. A separate team found harmful clots with a different formulation, showing why bleeding control and safety must be demonstrated together.
missing: Reliable, lasting control across severe artery and organ injuries still needs independent demonstration for each delivery route.
Treatment must keep working during transport and delayed surgery while leaving later repair feasible.
Safety must include nearby organs and circulation elsewhere in the body.
Trials before hospital arrival must establish improved survival and recovery in people.

milestones.label: Independent animal studies demonstrate lasting control across severe injuries
milestones.explanation: Blinded, independently repeated large-animal studies would have to show lasting control and survival across severe artery and organ injuries through delayed surgery, for each route. This would establish breadth and durability.

milestones.label: Benefits and harms meet thresholds set before testing
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to meet preset limits for control speed, rebleeding, survival, clots elsewhere, tissue damage and later repair. This would establish whether bleeding control comes with acceptable risks.

milestones.label: Trials before hospital arrival improve survival and recovery
milestones.explanation: Trials across multiple centres would have to improve survival and functional recovery under realistic conditions, including long transport. This would establish patient benefit and define the conditions in which treatment works.

uncertain: The treatable injuries, treatment window, required duration of control and acceptable safety thresholds remain undefined.
Success inside the abdomen does not establish success through the bloodstream; each route poses different safety and delivery problems.
The size of the survival benefit and the proportion of injured people who could benefit remain unknown.

page.title: Prehospital control of noncompressible abdominal hemorrhage
page.definition: A responder at the point of injury stops traumatic bleeding inside the abdomen that direct external pressure cannot reach, without needing to see the individual wound. Hemostasis, the cessation of bleeding, lasts through transport to surgery. The closest human example is ResQFoam, an investigational foam that expands inside the abdomen. Its sponsor reported treating a patient after arrival at a trauma center.

goal.need: Of 976 potentially survivable US battlefield deaths before arrival at a medical facility in October 2001–June 2011, 90.9% involved fatal bleeding. The torso accounted for 67.3% of lethal bleeding sites, and 64% of the truncal injuries involved the abdomen or pelvis. For wounded service members and civilian trauma patients, transfusion can sustain circulation while an internal wound continues to bleed. Stopping that loss during evacuation could reduce transfusion needs and keep patients alive until a surgeon can repair the injury.

completion.title: FDA approves a treatment for prehospital control of noncompressible abdominal hemorrhage.
completion.criterion: FDA grants marketing approval for point-of-injury treatment of noncompressible traumatic abdominal hemorrhage by nonsurgical responders, without direct visualization of the wound. Treatment maintains hemostasis during transport to surgery; an intracavity material can be removed at surgery. Eligible injuries, dosing and use conditions follow the approved indication.
completion.set_by: DARPA, Wound Stasis System programme, which states this goal for an abdominal stasis device; FDA supplies the marketing decision.
completion.threshold_quote: approval of a prototype device by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
completion.basis: DARPA connects its treatment goal to FDA approval. FDA evaluates safety and effectiveness for the intended use. The applicable device or drug pathway depends on product classification.

milestones.title: A candidate treatment demonstrates control of bleeding in laboratory injury models.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate preliminary control of bleeding in a laboratory injury model. For a drug or biologic, demonstrate preliminary efficacy in vivo. Identify the injury site and delivery route so that the finding can be judged for the model actually tested.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Defense, medical-device technology readiness level 3, and US Department of Health and Human Services, drug and biologic level 3C. The milestone uses the experimental component of each level.
milestones.threshold_quote: Generate preliminary in vivo proof-of-concept efficacy data

milestones.title: A candidate treatment demonstrates preclinical hemostatic activity and safety in defined animal models.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate hemostatic activity in an animal model relevant to traumatic abdominal bleeding and characterize the same candidate’s safety in defined animal models. Test activity under conditions consistent with the intended dose and route, and assess adverse effects of that exposure.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Defense, medical-device technology readiness level 4, and US Department of Health and Human Services, drug and biologic levels 4A and 4B. The milestone uses the preclinical experimental components.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of concept and safety of candidate device or system are demonstrated in defined laboratory or animal models.

milestones.title: A treatment reaches human use in an authorized investigation of traumatic abdominal hemorrhage.
milestones.criterion: At least one patient with traumatic abdominal hemorrhage receives the candidate in an investigation approved by the responsible institutional review board. A significant-risk device study requires an FDA-approved investigational device exemption. A drug investigation proceeds under an effective investigational new drug application. Treatment in hospital qualifies for this stage.
milestones.set_by: FDA, IDE Approval Process for significant-risk devices and the Investigational New Drug process for drugs. The quoted requirement concerns devices.
milestones.threshold_quote: the sponsor must also have an approved IDE from FDA prior to beginning the study at any site.

milestones.title: Pivotal human studies establish safety and effectiveness for the proposed prehospital indication.
milestones.criterion: One or more pivotal human investigations provide evidence of treatment benefit and an acceptable safety profile for the proposed prehospital use in traumatic abdominal hemorrhage. Judge benefit and harms against the endpoints and success criteria prespecified for that investigation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Design Considerations for Pivotal Clinical Investigations for Medical Devices, glossary definition of a pivotal study; Step 3: Clinical Research describes the corresponding drug treatment-benefit stage. The quoted definition concerns devices.
milestones.threshold_quote: A definitive study during which evidence is gathered to support the safety and effectiveness evaluation of the medical device for its intended use.

milestones.title: Animal dose-ranging studies identify an effective dose for abdominal hemorrhage.
milestones.criterion: Compare doses of the same candidate by its intended route in a relevant abdominal injury model. For a drug or biologic, identify the minimally effective dose. For an intracavity stasis material, identify a dose that balances bleeding control against injury caused by the material.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Health and Human Services, drug and biologic technology readiness level 5B, and DARPA, Wound Stasis System optimum-dosing objective for intracavity material.
milestones.threshold_quote: Identify minimally effective dose to facilitate determination of "humanized" dose once clinical data are obtained.

not_found: Programme documents and FDA guidance supplied no common numerical survival, blood-loss or thrombosis threshold for both delivery routes.
Searches of FDA material, trial records and developer updates located no marketing approval for the specified prehospital indication.
No registered prehospital pivotal protocol with a published numerical success boundary, or qualifying pivotal result, was located.
No human abdominal-hemorrhage investigation of SynthoPlate was located.
The archived DARPA WSS page gives no publication date.

results.finding: SynthoPlate achieved full hemostasis in 4 treated pigs by 80 minutes after femoral artery injury.
results.detail: The injury was in the femoral artery; the study does not establish efficacy in abdominal hemorrhage.
results.quote:
SynthoPlate –treated pigs 
exhibited significantly lower blood loss rates than comparison groups during the first 30 min and achieved full 
hemostasis (at 15 min, 18 min, 30 min and 80 min for the 4 pigs respectively) such that the blood loss rate for this 
group also became zero by the 80-minute time point (Fig. 6A).

results.finding: SynthoPlate showed hemostatic activity in 4 injured pigs and no alarming systemic risks in 2 uninjured pigs observed for 60 minutes.
results.detail: Safety observations were limited to a small group and short observation window; the injury model was femoral rather than abdominal.
results.quote:
Therefore, altogether these results suggest that within our experimental dose 
and animal observation window, administration of SynthoPlate did not cause any alarming systemic risks.

results.finding: Intraperitoneal hm-chitosan foam yielded 72% three-hour survival in swine with grade V hepatoportal injury (18 treated, 8 controls).
results.detail: Blood loss could not be accurately quantified. Intermittent fluid requirements after foam deployment suggested that some bleeding continued.
results.quote:
Three-hour survival was 72% in the
experimental group and 0% in the control group ( P ¼ .002).

results.finding: Intraperitoneal hm-chitosan foam sustained intra-abdominal pressure at 60–70 mmHg in a swine study with 18 treated animals and 8 controls.
results.detail: Follow-up ended at death or three hours. Gross examination addressed visible injury, while delayed effects and the consequences of pressure elevation remained unresolved.
results.quote:
Immediately after deployment,
intra-abdominal pressure increase rapidly and was sustained be-
tween 60 to 70 mmHg with a slight downward trend toward the
end of the 3-hour experiment.

results.finding: The swine study screened 15 intraperitoneal hm-chitosan foam formulations. The screening-only animal count was unreported.
results.detail: Selection favored mechanical integrity and prolonged survival. The reported concentration effects explain formulation selection but leave the dose-dependent injury tradeoff unresolved.
results.quote:
We evaluated 15 different hm-chitosan ebased foam formula-
tions to identify the one that had optimal mechanical integrity and
led consistently to signi ﬁcantly prolonged survival.

results.finding: Intravenous SynthoPlate achieved hemostasis in all 4 treated pigs with femoral artery injury by 80 minutes.
results.quote:
SynthoPlate –treated pigs 
exhibited significantly lower blood loss rates than comparison groups during the first 30 min and achieved full 
hemostasis (at 15 min, 18 min, 30 min and 80 min for the 4 pigs respectively) such that the blood loss rate for this 
group also became zero by the 80-minute time point (Fig. 6A).

results.finding: In the intravenous SynthoPlate safety study (6 uninjured pigs, 2 treated), organ histology found 0 off-target thrombi in treated animals.
results.detail: The dedicated safety study assessed acute effects over one hour. The efficacy study tested a single dose after an exposed femoral artery injury.
results.quote:
H&E staining-based 
histopathological analysis of harvested organs from SynthoPlate-injected un-injured animals showed no signs 
of off-target thrombi in the tissue samples (Fig.  4).

results.finding: In liver-injured swine (figure reports n=6/group), IV hemostatic nanoparticles at 2 mg/kg did not significantly reduce blood loss.
results.detail: The blood-loss figure reports six swine per group. The Methods list seven in the injured hemostatic nanoparticle arm and six in each injured control arm.
results.quote: There are no significant differences in blood loss over the time period studied for any of the groups.

results.finding: In liver-injured swine (figure reports n=6/group), IV hemostatic nanoparticles shortened prothrombin time (p<0.05).
results.detail: The uninjured arm had three swine per group. Pathology found thrombi in uninjured lungs, kidneys, or brain after nanoparticles. The coagulation figure reports six swine per injured group, while Methods list seven in the injured hemostatic nanoparticle arm.
results.quote: The prothrombin time (PT) is lower for the hNPs than for controls which suggests that the hNPs are hemostatic and reduce the time for blood to clot. (*p<0.05, error bars=SD)

results.finding: IV dF5 particles reduced blood loss after liver laceration in pigs versus saline (n=5 treated, n=4 saline, p=0.007).
results.detail: The experiment measured blood loss from a surgically exposed injury.
results.quote: total blood loss was significantly lower in PLP-treated animals compared to saline and platelet controls (saline vs dF5 PLPs p=0.007, platelets vs dF5 PLPs p=0.006)

results.finding: Pigs given IV dF5 particles after liver laceration (n=5 treated, n=4 saline) showed no off-target fibrin at day 7.
results.detail: The Results give 1 mg/kg for the porcine survival study. The Methods list 5 mL and 10 mg/kg for the same experiment.
results.quote: Histological analysis of peripheral organ tissue revealed no off-target fibrin formation or PLP presence one week after injury

results.finding: In mouse liver laceration, IV dF5 particles reduced blood loss versus saline at 10 mg/kg (n=5 per dose, n=6 saline).
results.detail: The mouse study used pretreatment and widely spaced doses. The post-injury pig experiments used a single dose per experiment.
results.quote: For all particle types, 10 mg/kg PLPs was identified as the optimal dose because it resulted in a significant (p<0.05) decrease in blood loss compared to saline controls

results.finding: Among 10 foam-treated swine with splenic injury, 1 developed postoperative ileus and was euthanized.
results.detail: Foam was removed after 3 hours. The report found no significant evidence of end-organ dysfunction or toxicity at either follow-up time point.
results.quote: One animal developed postoperative ileus and was euthanized; all other animals survived to the 28-day or 90-day end point without clinically significant complications.

results.finding: IHF achieved hemostasis in 28 s on average in the exposed rat liver wound model (n = 3 per group).
results.detail: The timed comparison used direct application to the exposed wound. The separate traumatic abdominal hemorrhage experiment used intracavity injection after the incision was sutured.
results.quote: Statistics showed the blood loss of foam without norepinephrine and IHF group were 0.24 ± 0.12 g and 0.114 ± 0.026 g, hemostasis time were 35.33 ± 9.29 s and 28 ± 7.94 s, respectively

results.finding: In rats with liver and spleen injuries (n = 3 in the removal protocol), no obvious adhesions were seen at 1 week after intracavity IHF removal.
results.detail: The source gives the rat sample size for the removal protocol. Group sizes for retained foam and the porcine cross-injury experiment are unspecified.
results.quote: No obvious postoperative adhesions were observed in all rats undergoing IHF therapy after 1 week

results.finding: One patient with traumatic abdominal bleeding received ResQFoam in the REVIVE study.
results.quote:
today announced the ﬁrst patient treated with a 
ﬁrst-of-its kind device, ResQFoam™, in the REVIVE clinical study at the University of 
Alabama at Birmingham (UAB).

results.finding: Swine with hepatoportal injury (n = 52) had a hemorrhage rate of 0.34 mL/kg/min in the highest-dose foam group.
results.quote:
Hemorrhage 
rate was reduced in all groups but lowest in Group 4 versus the control group (0.34 
[0.052] vs. 3.0 [1.3] mL/kg/min, p < 0.001).

results.finding: Swine with hepatoportal injury (n = 52) had a reported peak intra-abdominal pressure of 88.2 in the highest-dose foam group.
results.detail: The excerpt does not specify the pressure unit or give bowel injury counts by dose.
results.quote:
Increasing foam dose volume was 
associated with increased peak intra-abdominal pressure (88.2 [38.9] in Group 4 vs. 9.5 
[3.2] in the controls, p < 0.0001) and increased incidence of focal bowel injuries.

results.finding: Swine with hepatoportal injury (n = 52) had 90% three-hour survival in the highest-dose foam group.
results.detail: The highest dose gave the best bleeding and survival results. The reported increase in bowel injury and need for resection at higher doses leave the balance unresolved.
results.quote:
Survival with hepatoportal injury was highest in Group 4 (90%) and 
decreased in a dose-dependent fashion (Group 3, 72%; Group 2, 33%; Group 1, 17%).

results.finding: SynthoPlate rescue after mouse liver laceration yielded 0.69 g mean blood loss (n = 12 treated, 11 per control group).
results.detail: Time to hypotension was similar across rescue groups.
results.quote:
Administration of SynthoPlate
™
following liver laceration led a significant reduction in blood loss compared to control particles or saline (n=11 CP, n=12 SP, n=11 NS) (A).

results.finding: In liver-lacerated mice given intravenous SynthoPlate (n = 6), sampled organs accounted for about 25% of the injected dose.
results.detail: Biodistribution was measured after pretreatment. The discussion cites thrombosis-marker findings in uninjured mice from a separate study.
results.quote:
Finally, we quantified the clearance of SynthoPlate
™
from circulation in the setting of acute hemorrhage and found that only ~25% of injected particle dose was cleared at the time of sacrifice.

results.finding: In rats with liver hemorrhage (n unreported), Lyo-SP at 5 mg/kg significantly reduced blood loss and mortality.
results.quote: In contrast, rats dosed with 5 mg/kg Lyo-SP immediately (∼1 minute) or at 5 minutes post injury significantly reduced blood loss and mortality.

results.finding: In rats (n unreported), Lyo-SP was well tolerated up to 20 mg/kg, with no clotting detected in clearance organs.
results.detail: The intravenous case is inferred from the therapy context. The text does not establish that efficacy and safety were assessed by the intended route.
results.quote: In vivo, Lyo-SP was well tolerated in rats up to 20 mg/kg and showed no clotting risks in clearance organs, confirmed by histology.

results.finding: In rats with liver hemorrhage (n unreported), 5 mg/kg Lyo-SP was the lowest tested dose to significantly reduce blood loss and mortality.
results.quote: In contrast, rats dosed with 5 mg/kg Lyo-SP immediately (∼1 minute) or at 5 minutes post injury significantly reduced blood loss and mortality.

results.finding: IV dF5 platelet-like particles reduced blood loss after liver laceration in pigs versus saline (5 treated, 4 controls, p=0.007).
results.detail: Investigators measured blood loss with laparotomy sponges in an open surgical model.
results.quote: Animals that received PLPs had the least blood loss over time, and total blood loss was significantly lower in PLP-treated animals compared to saline and platelet controls (saline vs dF5 PLPs p=0.007, platelets vs dF5 PLPs p=0.006)

results.finding: IV dF5 platelet-like particles reduced blood loss in pigs with liver lacerations (5 treated, 4 saline controls), with safety monitored for 7 days.
results.detail: The Results give 1 mg/kg for the porcine studies, while the Methods describe injections as 5 mL of 10 mg/kg. The tested porcine dose cannot be resolved from the text.
results.quote: Histological analysis of peripheral organ tissue revealed no off-target fibrin formation or PLP presence one week after injury

results.finding: In mice with liver lacerations, prophylactic IV platelet-like particles reduced blood loss at 10 mg/kg (5 mice per formulation-dose group, 6 saline controls).
results.detail: The mouse study used three widely spaced doses before injury. The post-injury pig experiments used a single dose per study.
results.quote: For all particle types, 10 mg/kg PLPs was identified as the optimal dose because it resulted in a significant (p<0.05) decrease in blood loss compared to saline controls

results.finding: In a splenic hemorrhage study in swine (n = 20), the 150-mL intracavity foam group was terminated after the acute phase.
results.detail: The abstract cites prior hemostatic efficacy in a different swine injury model. The reported dose comparison establishes a tolerability limit and documents bowel injury requiring repair.
results.quote:
The 150-mL group was terminated after the acute phase (n = 
2).

results.finding: In 15 swine with severe splenic injury, the authors identified 20 mm Hg as the optimal abdominal gas insufflation pressure for bleeding control.
results.detail: The authors attributed worsening pH and lactate at higher pressures to possible iatrogenic abdominal compartment syndrome. Hemoperitoneum was measured at 30 minutes.
results.quote: Abdominal gas insufflation produced optimal bleeding control at 20 mm Hg.

results.finding: IV second-generation hemostatic nanoparticles stopped bleeding at 0.8 mg/kg in the sole pig tested at that dose after liver injury.
results.detail: The study tested lower doses of first-generation nanoparticles, a different formulation. Those results cannot establish the minimum effective dose of the second-generation candidate.
results.quote: In the lowest dose group, 0.8 mg/kg, the hemostatic nanoparticles lead to hemostasis at 15 minutes post injury

results.finding: In mice with liver lacerations (5 per FAMCY dose, 6 saline controls), 15 mg/kg IV FAMCY significantly reduced blood loss versus saline.
results.detail: A separate experiment found no significant difference between immediate post-injury and prophylactic administration. The reported dose comparison used pre-injury dosing.
results.quote: Total blood loss quantification over the course of the 10 minute injury showed significantly lower total blood loss for animals that received treatment with 15 mg/kg FAMCYs (0.0078 ± 0.003 gram blood/gram animal) compared to saline treated animals (0.016 ± 0.004 gram blood/gram animal, p-value = 0.0193)

results.finding: Among 149 TAMPITI patients analyzed, 53 in the intravenous tranexamic acid arms had an abdominal Abbreviated Injury Scale score of at least 3.

definition = "A responder at the point of injury stops traumatic bleeding inside the abdomen that direct external pressure cannot reach, without needing to see the individual wound. Hemostasis, the cessation of bleeding, lasts through transport to surgery. The closest human example is ResQFoam, an investigational foam that expands inside the abdomen. Its sponsor reported treating a patient after arrival at a trauma center.". Reason: The definition omits the traumatic cause and gives readers no clinical example distinguishing hospital use from treatment at the point of injury.

goal.need = "Of 976 potentially survivable US battlefield deaths before arrival at a medical facility in October 2001\u2013June 2011, 90.9% involved fatal bleeding. The torso accounted for 67.3% of lethal bleeding sites, and 64% of the truncal injuries involved the abdomen or pelvis. For wounded service members and civilian trauma patients, transfusion can sustain circulation while an internal wound continues to bleed. Stopping that loss during evacuation could reduce transfusion needs and keep patients alive until a surgeon can repair the injury.". Reason: The existing rationale omits the size of the affected group, the anatomical limits of the fatality data, and what stopping blood loss would add to transfusion.

add statement by Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, 2015: "non-compressible hemorrhage in the abdominal space, regardless of wound geometry or location within that space.". Reason: DARPA’s dated budget justification identifies both the abdominal target and the range of wounds the treatment was meant to reach.

add statement by International Delphi panel of military physicians, 2022: "Invasive bleeding control modalities should only be applied by trained physicians". Reason: The statements omit the military clinical panel’s reservation about who should administer invasive treatments such as abdominal foam.

edit m1: criterion = "Demonstrate preliminary control of bleeding in a laboratory injury model. For a drug or biologic, demonstrate preliminary efficacy in vivo. Identify the injury site and delivery route so that the finding can be judged for the model actually tested."; set_by = "US Department of Defense, medical-device technology readiness level 3, and US Department of Health and Human Services, drug and biologic level 3C. The milestone uses the experimental component of each level."; threshold_quote = "Generate preliminary in vivo proof-of-concept efficacy data"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [6, 7, 24]. Reason: The first milestone mixes study outcomes with the test and lacks the programme’s wording for preliminary efficacy.

edit m2: criterion = "Demonstrate hemostatic activity in an animal model relevant to traumatic abdominal bleeding and characterize the same candidate\u2019s safety in defined animal models. Test activity under conditions consistent with the intended dose and route, and assess adverse effects of that exposure."; set_by = "US Department of Defense, medical-device technology readiness level 4, and US Department of Health and Human Services, drug and biologic levels 4A and 4B. The milestone uses the preclinical experimental components."; threshold_quote = "proof of concept and safety of candidate device or system are demonstrated in defined laboratory or animal models."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 7, 25]. Reason: The second milestone substitutes findings from individual formulations for the programme’s test of activity and safety in defined models.

add milestone after m2: "Animal dose-ranging studies identify an effective dose for abdominal hemorrhage.". Reason: The sequence skips dose selection, a distinct preclinical question because greater bleeding control and greater tissue injury can occur at the same dose.

edit m3: criterion = "At least one patient with traumatic abdominal hemorrhage receives the candidate in an investigation approved by the responsible institutional review board. A significant-risk device study requires an FDA-approved investigational device exemption. A drug investigation proceeds under an effective investigational new drug application. Treatment in hospital qualifies for this stage."; threshold_quote = "the sponsor must also have an approved IDE from FDA prior to beginning the study at any site."; threshold_ref = 12; refs = [12, 13, 14]. Reason: The first-human-use criterion includes a sponsor announcement that belongs with the results and obscures whether in-hospital treatment qualifies at this stage.

edit m4: criterion = "One or more pivotal human investigations provide evidence of treatment benefit and an acceptable safety profile for the proposed prehospital use in traumatic abdominal hemorrhage. Judge benefit and harms against the endpoints and success criteria prespecified for that investigation."; threshold_quote = "A definitive study during which evidence is gathered to support the safety and effectiveness evaluation of the medical device for its intended use."; threshold_ref = 16; refs = [16, 13]. Reason: The pivotal criterion includes an in-hospital trial’s enrollment target and endpoint, neither of which sets the test for the prehospital indication.
